auxiliary_material: Study design: Randomized Phase II trial in metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients. Treatment context: Patients received gemcitabine, nab-paclitaxel, and cisplatin chemotherapy, NOT immune checkpoint inhibitors. Sample size: 32 evaluable patients total, but microbiome data from only 12 patients (4 MSKD group with 13 samples, 8 standard diet group with 23 samples). Statistical limitations: Alpha diversity difference not statistically significant (p=0.1339) due to small sample size. The authors state further validation in larger cohorts is warranted. Treatment response metrics (ORR, PFS, OS) are not explicitly defined in the abstract. This is not the DIET trial (NCT04645680); this is a separate pancreatic cancer chemotherapy study presented at AACR Special Conference 2025.

Study design is a prospective multicenter cohort of 95 Thai patients with advanced NSCLC receiving ICI (monotherapy or combination). Methods included shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool and 3-day food records. Specific taxa associated with shortened PFS included Firmicutes unclassified (HR 2.40), Ruminococcaceae family (HR 4.30), Intestinimonas genus (HR 2.61 in monotherapy subset), and Enterobacteriaceae family (HR 3.34 in monotherapy subset). Hyperprogressive disease (HPD) was defined as time to treatment failure < 2 months. Dietary pattern analysis used Diet Quality Index-International (DQI-I) and factor analysis identifying five patterns, with Pattern 3 (fats and dairy) showing a non-significant trend (P=0.07) towards association with HPD.

Does the DIET trial (NCT04645680) report specific gut microbiome taxonomic or functional changes that statistically mediate the observed clinical efficacy improvements in ICI-treated patients?

remaining_gap: Does the DIET trial (NCT04645680) or other human dietary intervention trials report specific gut microbiome compositional or functional changes that statistically mediate the observed clinical efficacy improvements in ICI-treated patients?
useful_material: This study reports specific gut microbiome compositional and functional changes associated with a medically supervised ketogenic diet (MSKD) intervention in humans. Taxonomical findings include significant enrichment of Akkermansia muciniphila (p=0.017931), Intestinimonas butyriciproducens (p=3.09E-05), Streptococcus thermophilus (p=1.15E-05), Roseburia hominis (p=3.94E-05), and Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus (p=7.28E-19) in the MSKD group compared to standard diet. Functional profiling identified increased phosphatidate metabolism (PWY-7039) and allantoin degradation (PWY-5705), with reduced L-ascorbate biosynthesis (PWY-6415). The authors note that Akkermansia muciniphila is linked to improved response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in existing literature. The study demonstrates that dietary intervention can produce sustained microbiome changes during cancer therapy, with MSKD patients showing better overall treatment responses and distinct microbiome profiles throughout therapy.

This study explicitly states in the Discussion section that 'Subsequent mediation analysis on gut microbiome was not able to be performed' due to limitations including small sample size for dietary data (N=34). It reports observational associations between baseline dietary patterns (specifically high fat and dairy intake) and gut microbiome composition (e.g., Firmicutes unclassified, Ruminococcaceae, Intestinimonas, Enterobacteriaceae) with ICI clinical outcomes (PFS, HPD status) in NSCLC patients. The authors note that while dietary patterns were associated with HPD, the sample size prevented statistical significance for diet-outcome links and precluded mediation modeling.
